specPoints.text: know that specific heat capacity is the energy required to change the temperature of an object by one degree Celsius per kilogram of mass (J/kg °C)
use the equation: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × change in temperature Δ Q = m × c × ΔT

primer.text: Different substances are differently stubborn about warming: water soaks up four thousand joules per kilogram per degree, metals far less. This note defines specific heat capacity, contrasts the high-capacity and low-capacity worlds, and drills the ΔQ = mcΔT calculation to a two-significant-figure finish.

lessons.title: Defining specific heat capacity
lessons.opening: Specific heat capacity is the price, in joules, of lifting one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius. High-capacity substances are slow to warm and slow to cool; low-capacity substances sprint through both.
keyPoints: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to warm 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.
Its unit is joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, written J/kg °C.
Water has a high specific heat capacity, so it warms up and cools down slowly.
Substances with a low specific heat capacity heat up and cool down quickly for the same energy.
The temperature change for a given energy input depends on the mass and the material heated.

low.restatement: Think of specific heat capacity as a per-kilogram, per-degree price tag. Water's tag is about 4200 J/kg °C, so a kettle needs thousands of joules for every single degree on every single kilogram.
low.analogy: Filling buckets of different widths: the same jug of energy raises the narrow bucket (low capacity) far faster than the wide one (high capacity).
low.examPointer: Always attach all three units — J/kg °C — because dropping the 'per kilogram' or the 'per degree' makes the definition wrong on the mark scheme.

medium.restatement: The definition is energetic, not thermal-intuitive: it is the energy per unit mass per unit temperature rise stored by the substance's particles. A high capacity means much of the supplied energy goes into the substance's internal store per degree, so temperature responds sluggishly in both heating and cooling directions.
medium.analogy: A wide harbour versus a narrow pool fed by the same stream: the harbour's level (temperature) creeps up while the pool leaps, even though the inflow (power) is identical.
medium.examPointer: Comparison questions want the consequence chain: higher capacity means slower warming AND slower cooling — quote both directions or the mark is half-earned.

check.stem: What is the definition of specific heat capacity?

options.text: the energy needed to warm 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
options.explanation: Per kilogram and per degree — the full definition.

options.text: the energy needed to melt 1 kg of a substance
options.explanation: That describes latent heat of fusion, not specific heat capacity.

options.text: the temperature rise produced by 1 joule in any mass
options.explanation: The definition fixes the mass at 1 kg and the rise at 1 °C.

options.text: the total energy stored in a heated object
options.explanation: That is thermal energy, not a per-kilogram-per-degree property.

check.stem: Which is the correct unit of specific heat capacity?

options.text: J/kg °C
options.explanation: Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius.

options.text: J/°C
options.explanation: That omits the per-kilogram part — heat capacity, not specific heat capacity.

options.text: W/kg °C
options.explanation: Watts measure energy per second, not energy.

options.text: J/kg
options.explanation: That omits the per-degree part.

check.stem: Two identical pans, one water and one oil, sit on identical flames. The oil warms faster. Why?

options.text: oil has a lower specific heat capacity than water
options.explanation: A smaller per-kilogram price means the same energy buys more degrees.

options.text: oil has a higher specific heat capacity than water
options.explanation: Higher capacity would make the oil warm more slowly.

options.text: the oil pan receives more energy
options.explanation: The flames are identical, so the energy supply is the same.

options.text: water always stays at the same temperature
options.explanation: Water warms too — just more slowly.

check.stem: Why is water used as a coolant in car engines?

options.text: its high specific heat capacity lets it absorb lots of energy for a small temperature rise
options.explanation: High capacity makes an excellent energy carrier.

options.text: its low specific heat capacity lets it heat up fast
options.explanation: Water's capacity is high, not low — and the cooling role wants that.

options.text: water conducts electricity around the engine
options.explanation: Pure water is a poor conductor and that is not the design goal.

options.text: water boils away to carry heat as steam
options.explanation: A coolant is meant to stay liquid, not boil off.

check.stem: A hot sand beach cools within minutes after sunset while the neighbouring sea stays warm for hours. Which property difference explains this?

options.text: sand's specific heat capacity is much lower than water's
options.explanation: Low capacity swings temperature quickly both ways.

options.text: sand's specific heat capacity is much higher than water's
options.explanation: High capacity would make sand the slow one.

options.text: the sea receives extra energy at night
options.explanation: Both lose energy after sunset; the capacities differ.

options.text: water cannot cool below air temperature
options.explanation: Water cools freely; it just does so slowly.

check.stem: State what a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C tells you about water.
check.modelAnswer: It takes 4200 joules of energy to raise the temperature of 1 kilogram of water by 1 °C.

check.stem: State whether a substance with a low specific heat capacity heats up quickly or slowly, and why.
check.modelAnswer: It heats up quickly, because only a little energy is needed per kilogram to raise its temperature by each degree.

check.stem: Explain why the same campfire warms a small iron kettle quickly but a large copper cauldron slowly, even though both metals have low specific heat capacities.
check.modelAnswer: The energy needed follows ΔQ = mcΔT, so mass matters as well as capacity. The kettle's small mass means the fire supplies its required energy quickly, while the cauldron's much larger mass multiplies the same per-kilogram price into a far larger total demand, so its temperature climbs slowly despite the low specific heat capacity.

check.stem: A 0.5 kg block of a metal with specific heat capacity 420 J/kg °C absorbs 21 000 J from a heater. Calculate its temperature rise.

lessons.title: Calculating with ΔQ = mcΔT
lessons.opening: One triangle equation runs the whole topic: change in thermal energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times temperature change. Rearranged, it also yields capacity from experiment data — the bridge to the core practical that follows this note.
keyPoints: The equation is ΔQ = m × c × ΔT for a temperature change with no change of state.
ΔQ is the change in thermal energy in joules, m the mass in kilograms, c the specific heat capacity, ΔT the temperature change in °C.
Rearranged forms give c = ΔQ ÷ (mΔT) and ΔT = ΔQ ÷ (mc).
Final answers should be quoted to an appropriate number of significant figures.
The equation applies only while the substance stays in one state — latent heat governs melting and boiling instead.

low.restatement: Multiply the mass by the capacity by the temperature change and you have the energy bill. Know any three of the four quantities and the fourth falls out by rearranging.
low.analogy: A restaurant bill: heads (mass) times set-menu price (capacity) times rounds (degrees) equals the total (energy).
low.examPointer: Write the equation first, substitute second, and quote units last — the three-line layout collects all the method marks.

medium.restatement: ΔQ = mcΔT quantifies the kinetic-energy store change of the particles: heavier samples and high-capacity substances demand proportionally more energy per degree. The rearrangement c = ΔQ/(mΔT) is exactly how the immersion-heater practical measures capacity, turning two meter readings and a thermometer into a material property.
medium.analogy: A toll road: total fare (ΔQ) scales with the number of vehicles (m), the per-vehicle rate (c), and the number of zones crossed (ΔT) — know three, recover the fourth.
medium.examPointer: Check the state before calculating: across a melting or boiling plateau ΔT is zero and the equation would wrongly return zero energy — that regime belongs to latent heat.

check.stem: Which equation gives the change in thermal energy with no change of state?

options.text: ΔQ = m × c × ΔT
options.explanation: Mass times capacity times temperature change.

options.text: ΔQ = m × L
options.explanation: That is the latent heat equation for state changes.

options.text: ΔQ = c × ΔT
options.explanation: The mass factor is missing.

options.text: ΔQ = m × c ÷ ΔT
options.explanation: The temperature change multiplies; it does not divide.

check.stem: In the equation ΔQ = m × c × ΔT, what are the units of each quantity?

options.text: J, kg, J/kg °C, °C
options.explanation: Energy, mass, capacity, temperature change — in that order.

options.text: W, kg, J/kg °C, K
options.explanation: ΔQ is energy in joules, not power in watts.

options.text: J, g, J/kg °C, °C
options.explanation: Mass must be in kilograms; grams need converting first.

options.text: J, kg, J/°C, °C
options.explanation: The capacity unit must keep its per-kilogram part.

check.stem: A kettle heats 0.48 kg of water by 0.7 °C. Taking c = 4200 J/kg °C, what energy is transferred?

options.text: about 1400 J
about 14 000 J
options.explanation: That overstates the product by a factor of ten.

options.text: about 140 J
options.explanation: That understates the product by a factor of ten.

options.text: about 2016 J
options.explanation: That forgets the 0.7 factor.

check.stem: A student computes a specific heat capacity of 42 000 J/kg °C for water from lab data. The accepted value is 4200. Which error best explains the tenfold result?

options.text: the mass was entered in grams instead of kilograms
options.explanation: c = ΔQ/(mΔT): a mass ten times too big makes c ten times too small — in reverse, an entry slip of units inflates it.

options.text: the temperature change was measured too accurately
options.explanation: Precision does not produce a tenfold bias.

options.text: water's capacity changes with the weather
options.explanation: Water's capacity is effectively constant across lab conditions.

options.text: the accepted value is wrong
options.explanation: 4200 J/kg °C is the established value.

check.stem: Why does ΔQ = mcΔT give zero energy across a melting plateau, and what replaces it there?

options.text: ΔT is zero during melting, so latent heat replaces the equation as the energy account
options.explanation: State changes are governed by latent heat, not by ΔQ = mcΔT.

options.text: the mass becomes zero during melting
options.explanation: Mass is conserved through a change of state.

options.text: c becomes infinite during melting
options.explanation: Capacity is defined within a single state.

options.text: no energy is supplied during melting
options.explanation: Energy is supplied — it funds the state change.

check.stem: State the equation linking the thermal energy change to mass, capacity and temperature change.
check.modelAnswer: ΔQ = m × c × ΔT — change in thermal energy equals mass times specific heat capacity times change in temperature.

check.stem: State the rearrangement used to find specific heat capacity from experimental data.
check.modelAnswer: Divide the measured energy by the product of mass and temperature change: c = ΔQ ÷ (m × ΔT).

check.stem: Explain why quoting 1411.2 J as 'about 1400 J' is better practice in an exam than leaving the long decimal.
check.modelAnswer: The inputs — 0.48, 0.7 — carry at most two significant figures, so the product cannot honestly carry more than two. Quoting 1400 J matches the precision of the data, avoids implying a false accuracy, and matches the mark scheme's expectation for rounded final answers.

check.stem: A 2.0 kg block of water-equivalent material at 20 °C is warmed to 50 °C by a 252 000 J input. Show that this is consistent with c = 4200 J/kg °C.
check.modelAnswer: ΔT = 50 − 20 = 30 °C, so ΔQ = m × c × ΔT = 2.0 × 4200 × 30 = 252 000 J — exactly the supplied energy, confirming the capacity value.

glossary.definition: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, in J/kg °C.
The internal energy of a substance associated with its particle motion and temperature.
The digits of an answer that carry meaningful precision given the inputs.

workedExample.prompt: Water of mass 0.48 kg is increased in temperature by 0.7 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the amount of thermal energy transferred to the water.
steps: List the known quantities: mass m = 0.48 kg, temperature change ΔT = 0.7 °C, specific heat capacity c = 4200 J/kg °C.
Write the relevant equation: ΔQ = m × c × ΔT.
Round the answer to 2 significant figures: ΔQ = 1400 J.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The thermal energy transferred to the water is 1400 J (2 s.f.).
